title: Block Size and the Three Kinds of Miss
unit: Memory Interfacing, Hierarchy and Cache Mapping
quickIdea: Every miss is compulsory (first touch), conflict (evicted by a block that shares its set) or capacity (the cache is simply too small); block size trades the first two against the miss penalty.
remember: Compulsory (cold) miss: the first access to a block, unavoidable whatever the cache size or organisation.
Conflict miss: a block that would have fit was evicted because another block mapped to the same set - direct mapping maximises these, full associativity eliminates them.
Capacity miss: the working set exceeds the cache, so a block is evicted even under full associativity.

The three are counted by running the same reference string three times: with an infinite cache (compulsory only), with full associativity of the real size (compulsory + capacity), and with the real organisation (all three).
Increasing the block size lowers compulsory misses by bringing neighbours along but raises the miss penalty and, past a point, raises conflict misses because the number of lines falls.

example.prompt: A 2 KB direct-mapped cache with 64 B blocks is given the sequence P, Q, R, S repeated, where P and S share a block and Q and R map to the same line as each other but not to P's. Classify the misses.
example.work: P: compulsory. S: hits, because it is inside P's block. Q: compulsory for line 10. R: conflict, because Q's line is taken. On each repetition P hits, Q misses again as a conflict with R, R misses as a conflict with Q, and S hits.
example.answer: One compulsory miss for P's block, one for Q's, and then a conflict miss on every Q and R access - 21 misses and 19 hits in the 40 accesses.

gateAngle: The three-way classification is GATE's favourite way to make a miss-count question conceptual, and the 2022 question is the clearest instance: two blocks thrash in one line while another line holds a block nobody else wants.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2022 Q.44: with P = 0xA248, Q = 0xC28A, R = 0xCA8A, S = 0xA262 in a 2 KB direct-mapped cache with 64 B blocks, which of 'every access to S is a hit', 'P is never evicted', 'only R and S remain at the end', 'every access to R evicts Q' are true?
variations.answer: The first, second and fourth are true; the third is false because P's block is still resident.
variations.why: P and S share index 9 with tag 20, so the block is never disturbed; Q and R share index 10 with different tags, so they evict each other on every pass.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Same sequence and cache, but the cache is made 2-way set-associative. What happens to the misses?
variations.answer: Q and R now sit in the two ways of their set, so both survive and neither evicts the other. The trace has three compulsory misses - P, Q and R are three distinct blocks and each is touched for the first time once - and 37 hits.
variations.why: It isolates the conflict misses by removing exactly the constraint that caused them: with two ways the Q-R thrashing disappears, and what is left is the compulsory misses that no organisation can remove.

trap.what: Assuming a conflict miss and a capacity miss are the same thing.
trap.why: A conflict miss disappears if the associativity is raised at the same cache size; a capacity miss does not, because the cache is genuinely too small.
trap.counterexample: The 2022 sequence on a 2 KB cache: making it fully associative removes the Q-R thrashing entirely (conflict), while a 64 B cache of any associativity still cannot hold all four blocks (capacity).

check.question: A program touches 300 distinct blocks in a 128-line fully associative cache, each exactly once. How many misses, and of what kind?
check.answer: 300 misses, all compulsory; capacity is irrelevant because no block is re-read, and there are no conflicts because the cache is fully associative.
check.explanation: The miss rate is 1 here for a reason the classification makes obvious: with no reuse there is nothing for a cache to exploit.
